en: The *Buddha-sūtra on the Prince’s Mupò*, as recorded in the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu*, states:
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Zhu Fahu of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin dynasty; titled *Mupò* or *Mupo*.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, and addressed [the assembly].
The monks: "In the past, there was a king named Vārāṇasī.
The king had a crown prince named Mūpaka, who possessed infinite wisdom from birth; he was upright, exquisite, and pure, with no equal to compare him."
His parents marveled at him and provided for him with constant care, waiting until he had grown up so that they might bestow a name upon him.
Yet the Prince remained mute, unable to speak, for thirteen years; he was serene, simple, and plain, his will like extinguished ashes and his mind like withered wood.
His eyes did not gaze upon forms, nor did his ears listen to sounds; his appearance was like that of one who is mute, deaf, and blind.
Thereupon, his parents grew weary of him and were distressed.
The King said to the Queen,
"What should we do about him?"
"This child will surely be ridiculed by other countries.
The lady said to the king,
"We should summon a physiognomist to examine him and find out whether he will speak or not."
The king immediately summoned his brahmin master and ordered him to examine the crown prince.
The brahmin said, "This child is not an ordinary person of the world; he is merely a malevolent planet."
Outwardly he appears upright, but inwardly he harbors ill omen;
the ruin of the state and the extinction of his clan will arrive before long.
He must not be kept; he should be buried alive and executed.
"If we do not spare this son, the succession of the state will be cut off.
The King said to the Queen, "What should be done?"
"If we do not remove this son now, I fear that in the future there will be no one to establish as the Crown Prince.
Thereupon, the lady followed the King's lead.
The King immediately summoned the great ministers of the realm to deliberate upon the matter together.
One minister said,
"He should be banished far away to the deep mountains, to a place where no people dwell.
Another minister said:
"One should drown him in deep water.
Another minister said, "One should simply follow what the teacher says: dig a deep pit and bury him alive."
The king immediately followed the words of this minister; he summoned more than three thousand soldiers from the outer ranks and ordered them to dig the earth to create a storehouse.
He provided the prince with worldly provisions and attended him with five servants, returning all the prince’s robes, necklaces, and precious jewels to him.
Thereupon, the wife’s heart was filled with grief and despair:
"I alone am without fortune; my son is ill-fated, and having met with this calamity, our affairs cannot be brought to an end."
With tears streaming down and voices choked with sobs, they could not restrain themselves.

Thereupon, they escorted the Prince once more to the main hall. Upon seeing that the Prince was so upright, handsome, and peerless, the five hundred ladies all said, "Why does the Prince remain silent? Why must he be buried alive?"
When the five hundred court ladies saw that the Prince was upright and handsome, they all paid homage to him and said, "Why did you not speak to us?
Why would you bury yourself alive?"
Each performed their respective musical performances for the Prince.
The Prince remained silent, neither looking nor listening.
They then escorted the Prince to the outer palace hall; seeing that the Prince was upright, handsome, and peerless, the five hundred ministers came forward and addressed the Great King:
"The Prince is not a man who remains silent; let him stay for a while longer, and he will speak before long.
The Brahmin said, "This cannot be trusted as certain."
The King said to his ministers, "This is a matter of state; it is not for you to know.
Once the treasury had been completed, he came to welcome the Prince.
The king said to his attendant:
"Have the crown prince mount my four-sided elephant chariot and let the people of the kingdom come to see him; the prince shall speak.
If he speaks, then bring him back here."
Thereupon, the Prince mounted his carriage and set out along the road.
The elders and senior ministers of the kingdom all prostrated themselves before the carriage and said: "Prince!..."
"You must speak a single word.
If you do not speak, I shall simply drive my carriage over you.
Caeli the Halberdier supported him and helped him avoid the path so that the carriage could pass by.
He then attended upon the Prince and proceeded to the place where the treasury was located.
At that time, there were several tens of millions of people who all followed the Prince to the treasury, completely blocking its doors so that the Prince could not advance further.
When Cāṇūra and the *varmiṇa* warriors brandished their banners, the people retreated.

Just as the Prince advanced, birds in flight and wild beasts in their tracks were startled and rushed forward again; they circled the treasury three times and once more blocked its door, so that the Prince could not proceed further.
Thereupon, the Prince raised his right hand, paused, and said:
"If I do not speak, I shall be buried alive;
yet if I were to speak now, I fear I would fall into hell."
The reason I do not speak is that I wish to keep my body at peace and avoid harm, and to deliver my spirit from suffering; for this reason, I remain silent.
Yet you believe in deceptive and fraudulent words, claiming that my deafness and blindness are real, and that I am truly mute.
At that time, the people heard the Prince’s words, which were of such exquisite beauty that they were rarely heard in the world; those walking stopped, and those sitting rose, all saying:
"The Prince is so divine and holy!"
They all came forward, prostrating with their heads to the ground, seeking grace and repenting for their transgressions, entreating him to pardon their offenses.
When his servants heard this, they were filled with joy and leaped for gladness; they ran to inform the Great King:
"The Prince has already spoken; his words have reached up to the azure heavens and down to the Yellow Springs."
"Even the birds and beasts all came to prostrate and listen before the Prince.
When the King heard the Prince's words, he was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he immediately set out with his consort in a four-wheeled elephant chariot to go and welcome the Prince.
The Crown Prince looked back toward his father, the King, descended from his carriage, stepped aside to clear the path, and after performing four prostrations, he spoke:
"I am weary that my father, the King, has condescended to come so far to welcome me.
Today, father and son have already become estranged; our affection has been severed and our kinship divided. This is a profound transgression of righteousness, and I cannot bear to look upon it."
The king said to the crown prince: "No! No!"
"You are a wise man; you should forgive my shortcomings.
Let us return together to the kingdom, and I shall offer the throne to you while I myself withdraw.
The prince replied:
"In a former life, I was a king; because my conduct was deficient, I fell into hell for more than sixty thousand years, where I was steamed, boiled, flayed, and torn apart—the pain was unbearable."
At this time, would my parents truly be able to know the intensity of my suffering in hell?
Would they truly be able to share in the pain upon my body?

I loathe and fear the suffering of hell; for this reason, I have remained tongue-tied and silent for thirteen years, hoping thereby to escape blemish, remove defilement, emerge beyond the dust of the world, and not encounter further transgression.
Eliminate sorrow and cast off burdens; regard life as a temporary lodging.
One cannot choose to be weak, for then one drifts further and further from the Way.
Soaring high and traveling far, one brings oneself to salvation within this world.
The world is impermanent, as fleeting and illusory as a dream;
the joys and pleasures of the family last but a moment;
happiness is but temporary, while sorrow and suffering endure for long.
"Knowing that the Crown Prince’s intention was firm and his resolve steadfast, the King finally permitted him to study the Way.
Thereupon, the Crown Prince abandoned his kingdom and renounced his kingship; he entered the mountains to seek the Way, contemplating in meditative concentration."

At the end of his life, he was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven; after completing his lifespan there, he descended to be born in the world as the crown prince of the King of Kapilavastu, where he attained Buddhahood by himself.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"At that time, the prince Mūkapāla was my own self;
at that time, the father-king was the present King Śuddhodana."
The mother at that time was none other than Māyā;
the five attendants who served me then were Ājñātakauṇḍinya and the others;
and the brahmin who wished to bury me alive was none other than Devadatta. Thus, Devadatta and I have harbored enmity throughout successive lifetimes.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, all the disciples, devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, and common people were filled with great joy and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Sutra on the Prince’s Death Spoken by the Buddha.
